narrative:
The model determined that you have a 74% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons for the negative outcome. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3 strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. These early and later academic standings were the two most influential pieces of information the model considered. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor. Although your score of 34 was only a few points below the average of accepted students (37), it still nudged the prediction slightly toward passing rather than failure.

In short, the model saw your consistently low class rankings as clear signals that you would struggle with the bar exam, and this outweighed the modestly encouraging effect of your LSAT performance.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking key courses to raise your GPA, which currently sits at 2.9 compared with 3.23 for accepted students, and invest time in intensive LSAT preparation to improve that score. With clearer evidence of stronger performance, a future application would be viewed much more favorably. (218 words)
